data.title: Grab to buy 60% stake in Atome Financial for $1.49B
data.description:
Grab Holdings (GRAB) has agreed to acquire a controlling 60% stake in Atome Financial for $1.49B in cash, expanding its digital lending business across Southeast Asia.

The transaction includes $260M of primary growth capital and is expected to close by the third quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary conditions. Grab will consolidate Atome Financial into its Financial Services segment following the deal.

Atome Financial, the digital financial services platform of Advance Intelligence Group (AIGL), offers buy now, pay later (BNPL) loans, consumer cash loans, BNPL cards and digital lending across Singapore, Malaysia, the Philippines, Indonesia and Thailand. The platform has served 25M cumulative transacted users.

The acquisition will give Grab access to Atome Financial’s established consumer lending platform, while Atome Financial will gain expanded distribution through Grab’s mobility, deliveries and financial services ecosystem.

Grab has also agreed to acquire the remaining 40% stake approximately two years after the Phase 1 closing. The second transaction will be based on Atome Financial’s performance rather than a fixed price, using a valuation formula based on annualized adjusted EBITDA and revenue.

The resulting equity valuation will have a floor of $2B and a cap of $4.5B, with at least 50% of the consideration payable in cash.

data.title: Six consumer stocks in harm's way if Super El Niño is as bad as feared
data.description:
Jefferies warned that the consumer sector that could be impacted by a Super El Niño this year and into 2027.   

Current forecasts suggest the 2026-27 El Niño may be the strongest in modern history, according to the firm. It was noted that, unlike most climate risks, El Niño is highly trackable months in advance, giving investors an opportunity to identify economic consequences before they fully materialize.

Hershey (HSY): Analyst Scott Marks warned Hershey (HSY) carries concentrated cocoa exposure through its core U.S. chocolate portfolio and has built its 2027 margin recovery plan around expected cocoa deflation. "Notably, a Super El Niño driving a hotter, drier West African 2026/27 crop would undercut the central pillar of the recovery story," updated Marks. 

Jefferies named the below consumer stocks as part of a larger multi-sector list of names at risk of Super El Niño disruption.

J.M. Smucker (SJM): The food company is exposed to El Niño through its coffee portfolio. The company's sourcing could be impacted for Brazilian arabica and Vietnamese/Indonesian robusta.

Mondelez International (MDLZ): The Chicago-based food giant is seen having El Niño exposure runs through cocoa, with ~60% of supply in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana, where strong events historically turn hotter and drier heading into the Nov-Jan harvest. The risk is that a Super El Niño hitting the 2026/27 crop would threaten the margin recovery narrative.

PriceSmart (PSMT): Analyst Pedro Baptista noted that the retailer derives approximately 11% of sales from Colombia and also operates across Central America, making it exposed to weather-related disruptions, supply chain interruptions and weaker discretionary spending in affected markets. "While individual warehouses may experience temporary operational impacts, previous events suggest demand is often deferred rather than destroyed, with recovery supported by the company's membership-based model and resilient consumer positioning," advised Baptista.

Yum China (YUMC): Analyst Anne Ling noted extreme rainfall, flooding, and adverse weather may temporarily reduce dine-in traffic at stores, particularly in affected regions, and disrupt logistics and delivery efficiency. Meanwhile, restaurants could face higher prices for key agricultural inputs. 

Coca-Cola FEMSA (KOF): Analyst Alex Wright highlighted that a sharp rise in sweetener costs could pressure margins if cost increases outpace pricing actions.

data.title: Rocket Lab locks in financing for planned Iridium acquisition
data.description:
Rocket Lab (RKLB) has raised $1.944B in gross proceeds from its at-the-market share sale, issuing 29.3M shares to help finance its pending acquisition of Iridium Communications (IRDM).

The company said the proceeds, together with Iridium’s existing term loan and other available funds, are sufficient to fund the required cash consideration and related transaction costs.

Iridium amended its existing $1.775B credit facility to permit the change of control, providing long-term financing backed by its free cash flow and a parent guarantee from Rocket Lab USA.

Rocket Lab also terminated its $3.6B bridge facility, de-risking the capital structure ahead of the planned mid-2027 close of the Iridium acquisition.

data.title: Iran war cost: $33.4B in four months, U.S. munitions shortfalls
data.description:
The Iran war has cost an estimated $33.4B as of June 29, according to a report on Operation Epic Fury (OEF) from the Lead Inspector General of the Department of Defense that was submitted to Congress.

This estimate includes $22.3B for expended munitions, $7.4B of cumulative obligations (incremental costs) for OEF and $3.7B in equipment losses. It does not include costs for infrastructure repairs, the report noted.

The munitions expenditure has "resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply," the Office of the Under Secretary for Acquisition and Sustainment stated.

The Pentagon said it did not include the cost of construction for damaged infrastructure in its estimate as it "has not determined what its future posture will be in the region, how it will construct its bases and what percentage of the construction costs Allies and partners will contribute."

Iranian strikes destroyed or damaged dozens of U.S. aircraft and drones, including four F-15E fighter jets (BA), one F-35A (LMT) and one A-10. Notably, the F-35A costs ~$92M per plane and the F-15E costs over $60M per unit.

Hundreds of buildings and structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan were also damaged. 

The cost of damages to U.S. diplomatic facilities in Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the UAE is estimated at ~$184M.

Seven U.S. Service members were killed in action from Feb. 28 to June 30, seven were killed in non-hostile events during OEF combat operations and 417 service members were wounded in action, the report noted.

data.title: Fed unlikely to hike rates this week despite 87% market odds
data.description:
The Federal Reserve is unlikely to raise interest rates at its September meeting despite financial markets pricing in a high probability of a hike, according to Michael R. Strain, Director of Economic Policy Studies and Senior Fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.

Strain said the “center of gravity” of the Federal Open Market Committee remained tilted toward holding rates at its July meeting, and he does not believe the economic data released since then have been strong enough to materially change that view.

Strain acknowledged that the August consumer price index report could have shifted some FOMC members toward favoring a rate increase, but argued that the data would have needed to be significantly more concerning to prompt the Fed to begin a new hiking cycle.

He noted that markets were pricing an 87% probability of a hike, but said the appropriate question is not simply whether the Fed should raise rates this week, but whether it should begin a hiking cycle.

The possibility of a one-and-done increase, he added, would create a separate communications challenge for Chairman Warsh, who may not want to explain why the Fed delivered its first isolated rate hike in decades.

The August inflation data, meanwhile, may not be as troubling as the market reaction suggests, Strain said. Based on the CPI report, he expects August monthly core PCE inflation to accelerate somewhat from June and July, but still come in around 3.1% annualized, with the six-month change in core PCE at roughly 3.2% annualized.

If those estimates hold, Strain believes most FOMC members could still view the data as consistent with ongoing disinflation rather than a meaningful reacceleration in inflation. Core services CPI was 3% year-over-year in August, unchanged from July, offering little evidence of a renewed acceleration in underlying services inflation.

Strain also argued that financial conditions have tightened over the past several weeks, potentially doing some of the work that a higher federal funds rate would otherwise accomplish.

While avoiding a negative market reaction can be a consideration for policymakers, he said a one-and-done hike would itself run counter to market expectations, with bond markets pricing in roughly a 75% probability of two or more rate increases in 2026.

A hike would therefore still risk surprising markets unless the Fed intended to signal that its policy approach under Warsh would differ from that of its recent predecessors.

Despite his expectation that the Fed will hold rates this week, Strain said he personally would favor an increase. He said the federal funds rate is too low and that he would have voted for a hike in July, having also opposed the Fed’s rate cuts in 2025.

However, he does not believe the majority of the FOMC has materially changed its assessment since July, leading him to expect the central bank to leave rates unchanged this week, while acknowledging that he “would not be shocked” if the Fed ultimately raises rates.

data.title: AM Markets Need to Know: China tightens AI safeguards, bond yields rise, and more
data.description:
Stock index futures were lower on Tuesday while Treasury yields rose as traders looked forward to the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision later in the week.

Here are the five news items investors should watch:

China steps up AI safeguards: Beijing is taking increasing measures to guard against increasingly capable AI systems escaping human control, seeking to manage risks without curbing the technology's rapid expansion. The move comes as Anthropic (ANTHRO) CEO Dario Amodei has urged AI companies to slow model development, and the company has disclosed cases involving AI models being used in cyber weapons and other high-risk activities.

10-year Treasury yield hits 2007 high: The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield (US10Y) climbed to 5.03% Tuesday, surpassing its 2023 peak and reaching its highest level since 2007. Rising oil prices, heavier government debt, and renewed inflation concerns are driving a broader global bond selloff, increasing pressure on equity valuations and borrowing costs.

Rate hikes could trigger S&P 500 correction: Macro Risk Advisors expects potential Federal Reserve rate hikes to trigger an 8%-10% correction in the S&P 500 (SP500), with another decline possible in December. CEO Dean Curnutt said higher rates could pressure corporate margins, weaken earnings expectations, and increase volatility if companies cannot pass higher costs to customers.

Trump dismisses AI takeover concerns: President Donald Trump called concerns over AI a “hoax” during a surprise call with Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang at the All-In Summit. Trump also argued that data centers will generate wealth and said the U.S. should maintain its AI lead over China, underscoring the administration's focus on accelerating development.

Clarity Act odds fall as crypto rally stalls: Polymarket odds of the Clarity Act passing this year fell to 18% from above 30% during U.S. trading, weighing on crypto sentiment. Bitcoin (BTC-USD) retreated from nearly $79,600 to below $78,000 as Democratic negotiators prepared a counteroffer to Republicans ahead of a key procedural vote.

data.title: Amazon sets Oct. 6-7 for Prime Big Deal Days
data.description:

data.title: Former DeepMind researcher adds to warnings that AI threat may be growing
data.description:
A former Google (GOOG) (GOOGL) DeepMind employee on Monday became the latest AI researcher to warn that the technology could potentially “kill all humans,” saying the window to prevent such an outcome may be narrowing.

The comments come after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said last week he had resigned, in part because the "people building AI earnestly believe that it could ​kill us all by the end of the decade." Anthropic scientist ​Evan Hubinger then responded to Coxon's comments, saying he was correct ⁠and that he believed there was a greater than 10% chance ​that AI could kill all humans within the next decade.

"I recently resigned from ​Google DeepMind, where I worked on AGI safety and alignment research," Bilal Chughtai wrote on X. "I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all, and ​that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome."

Chughtai, ​who co-authored research papers while at Google DeepMind, worked there as a research engineer ‌and ⁠left the company this year in July, according to his LinkedIn profile.

Following recent concerns, Anthropic (ANTHRO) CEO Dario Amodei called for a slowdown in the pace of advanced ​AI development, winning ⁠rare backing from SpaceXAI's (SPCX) Elon Musk and OpenAI (OPENAI) CEO Sam Altman and sparking a debate over AI "doomerism."

President Donald Trump, however, ​has dismissed the warnings, saying on social media the AI industry's call for regulation is a "hoax."

data.title: Sasol signs SAF supply deal with White Desert for Antarctic flights - report
data.description:
Sasol (SSL) signed a fuel supply agreement with Antarctic operator White Desert to support flights to Antarctica, giving the South African energy and chemicals group a new aviation-fuel customer in the specialist polar travel market.

The deal follows Sasol receiving independent certification from German agency TÜV SÜD in April for its SAF. The co-processed fuel is made using cooking oil and vegetable oil at Sasol’s 108,500-barrel-per-day Natref refinery, which primarily processes crude oil.

White Desert previously sourced SAF from Europe but switched to Sasol after the company received local certification, a senior official said, Reuters reported. White Desert operates one flight a week from Cape Town to Antarctica during its November-February season, with its first flight using Sasol’s SAF on an Airbus A340-600 expected in November.

The financial terms of the agreement were not disclosed. Sasol (SSL) did not provide the contract value, pricing, supply volume, or expected revenue impact.

The agreement adds to Sasol’s (SSL) efforts to expand its SAF business as it works to develop lower-carbon fuel options.
